prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue, Nor swifter greyhound follow, Whose foot ne’er tainted morning dew, Nor ear heard huntsman’s hallo’, Old Tiney, surliest of his kind, Who, nursed with tender care, And to domesticate bounds confined, Was still a wild jack-hare. Though duly from my hand he took His pittance every night, He did it with a jealous look, And, when he could, would bite. His diet was of wheaten bread, And milk, and oats, and straw, Thistles, or lettuces instead, With sand to scour his maw. On twigs of hawthorn he regaled, On pippins’ russet peel; And, when his juicy salads failed, Sliced carrot pleased him well. A Turkey carpet was his lawn, Whereon he loved to bound, To skip and gambol like a fawn, And swing his rump around. His frisking was at evening hours, For then he lost his fear; But most before approaching showers, Or when a storm drew near. Eight years and five round-rolling moons He thus saw steal away, Dozing out all his idle noons, And every night at play. I kept him for his humor’s sake, For he would oft beguile My heart of thoughts that made it ache, And force me to a smile. But now, beneath this walnut-shade He finds his long, last home, And waits in snug concealment laid, Till gentler Puss shall come. He, still more agèd, feels the shocks From which no care can save, And, partner once of Tiney’s box, Must soon partake his grave.

### Option 1: Elevated Literary Prose (Recommended)

> Here lies Tiney, a wild jack-hare who never knew the chase of a hound nor the sound of a huntsman’s call, and whose feet never disturbed the morning dew. Raised with tender care within the comforts of a home, he nevertheless remained the surliest of his kind. A Turkish carpet served as his meadow, where he loved to leap, gambol like a fawn, and spin about. >
> For eight years and five months, he spent his life dozing through idle afternoons and playing through the nights. I kept him for his unique disposition, as he frequently lifted my spirits, distracting me from grief and bringing a smile to my face. 
>
> Now, he rests permanently in the shade of a walnut tree, awaiting the arrival of Puss—a gentler and even older hare who once shared his box, and who must soon succumb to the frailties of age to join Tiney in his final resting place.

### Option 2: Refined Poetic Verse

> Here lies a hare no hound did e'er pursue,  
> Nor swift greyhound chase, nor huntsman’s halloo;  
> Whose feet did never taint the morning dew.  
> Old Tiney—surliest of his wild domain—  
> Though raised with tender care and gentle rein,  
> Remained a untamed jack-hare to the last.  
> 
> Though from my hand his nightly food was passed,  
> He took his meal with a suspicious glare,  
> And bit my fingers when I was unaware.  
> His diet offered wheaten bread and milk,  
> With straw and oats, and lettuces like silk;  
> Thistles he ate, and sand to scour his maw,  
> Hawthorn and apple peels within his paw,  
> And sweet sliced carrots when his greens grew rare.  
> 
> A Turkey carpet was his meadow green,  
> Where he would leap and gambol on the scene—  
> Like a young fawn he spun and played around.  
> At dusk his lively spirits would abound,  
> For nightfall eased his fear, but most of all  
> When rain approached or storms began to fall.  
> 
> For eight long years and five full moons he stayed,  
> Dozing all noon, while every night he played.  
> I kept him for his humor, for his art  
> Could chase away the sorrows of my heart  
> And force a smile when I was weighed with grief.  
> 
> Now 'neath the walnut shade he finds relief,  
> Laid in snug sleep until his friend shall come—  
> For gentler Puss, now aged, frail, and numb,  
> Who shared his box through all the years gone by,  
> Must soon beside his former partner lie.

Old Tiney was no ordinary creature; born a wild jack-hare, his life diverted dramatically from the typical fate of his kind. Rather than running from hounds or enduring the perils of the open fields, he found sanctuary as a protected domestic pet, rescued from the wild to live a life of comfort and safety. 

Yet, despite receiving tender care, lavish attention, and a rich, varied diet, Tiney never entirely shed his wild nature. He remained stubbornly surly and suspicious throughout his life, frequently repaying his owner’s kindness with an unexpected nip. He was a creature who accepted his luxurious surroundings entirely on his own terms, refusing to yield his fiery independence to domestic softness.

His daily routine followed a peculiar, charming rhythm. Tiney spent the daylight hours peacefully asleep, but as evening fell, he would awaken into a burst of joyous energy, playfully leaping and bounding across the living room carpet. He was also remarkably attuned to nature, acting as a living weather glass who became wildly active and restless in the hours leading up to an approaching storm.

For over eight years, Tiney’s entertaining antics and brooding charm brought profound warmth to his home. During times of personal grief and dark, sorrowful days, the eccentric hare provided his owner with immense comfort, bringing smiles and laughter when they were needed most. 

Sadly, Old Tiney’s long and memorable journey has now come to an end. Having recently passed away, he was laid to rest in a peaceful grave beneath the shade of a walnut tree. Though his presence is deeply missed, his memory remains bright—and in time, his surviving elderly companion hare will be laid to rest beside him under the same quiet branches.
outputs.L4:
Of all the creatures that ever crossed the threshold of my home, none presented so fierce a challenge to my patience as Old Tiney. A jack-hare caught from the heath, he possessed an inherent, unyielding savagery—a spirit forged by the drafty fields and the constant instinct to flee or fight. When I first brought him indoors, he was a tempest of thumping hind legs, bared teeth, and flattened ears, desperately resisting any attempt at human touch. Yet, seeing in him a wild beauty that deserved protection, I resolved to turn my home into his sanctuary and win whatever measure of his trust he might spare.

Domesticating a beast so thoroughly wild required an exacting, almost obsessive devotion. I fashioned a safe haven for him within my own living quarters, entirely free from the drafty corners, hunting hounds, and lurking predators that shadowed his wild brethren. His daily care became a strict, beloved ritual. I catered to his capricious appetite with a varied and meticulous diet, foraging daily for his favorite delicacies. His trough was never without crisp sprigs of garden parsley, bitter dandelion leaves freshly harvested in the morning dew, crunchy oats, sweet slices of apple, and the tenderest green barks of young saplings. Under this vigilant protection and endless bounty, Tiney flourished physically, growing sleek, strong, and healthy.

Yet, for all my efforts, Tiney refused to surrender his native sullenness. He was, to his very core, a hopelessly surly creature. Where another animal might have softened into docility after years of gentleness, Tiney maintained an ironclad grudge against his capter. He regarded my hand not as a source of warmth, but as an enemy to be avoided or chastised. To reach out and stroke his soft coat was to invite a sharp nip or an indignant, echoing thump of his powerful foot upon the floorboards. He accepted my meticulously prepared meals with a look of stern entitlement, offering not a single gesture of affection in return. For eight long years, he lived under my roof as a glorious, unrepentant grudge-holder.

And yet, I grew to treasure him immensely, for a strange magic overtook Old Tiney as the sun dipped below the horizon. When night fell and the oil lamps were lit, the surly recluse of the daytime vanished. In his place emerged a creature of sudden, frantic delight. The parlor became his private arena, and Tiney would break into the most absurdly joyful evening antics. He would execute magnificent, twisted leaps over the furniture, race in furious circles across the rug, and engage in mock battles with unseen foes, his long ears flopping wildly as he gamboled through the room. 

It was during these twilight hours that the true depth of our unspoken bond was forged. In those years, my heart was weighed down by a severe, dark melancholia—a persistent sorrow that threatened to consume my thoughts whenever the house grew quiet. I was powerless to heal myself, but I found an unexpected cure in Tiney’s foolish, fiery evening dances. Watching his wild, unpredictable displays broke the grip of my despondency, pulling my mind away from its internal grief and forcing me into the light of the present moment. His comical vigor was a vital tonic; he gave me laughter when I had none left of my own.

When Old Tiney finally succumbed to old age after eight years in my care, I mourned him deeply. He died as he had lived: stubborn, fierce, and entirely his own master. He never truly learned to love me, nor did he ever tame his wild, belligerent spirit to suit human desire. Yet, in his endless, grumpy independence, and in the fleeting beauty of his evening games, he had rescued me from the depths of my own dark sorrow, proving that even the wildest heart can offer profound comfort to a lonely soul.

Here rests beneath this mossy mound
A creature surly, wild, and proud;
Though safe from huntsman and the hound,
He wore a dark, disdainful shroud.

’Twas Tiney called—of savage strain,
Whose moody brow no love could tame;
He viewed my kindness with disdain,
And fled my hand, and scorned his name.

Yet eight long years he shared my hearth,
A captive by his own decree;
The fiercest leveret on the earth,
Who spurned all human amity.

Strange were his ways when shadows fell,
And firelight flickered on the hall;
He’d leap as drawn by magic spell,
To box his shadow on the wall.

With sudden thump and furious glare,
He’d scowl beneath the cushioned seat—
A most unaccountable hare,
Who answered mercies with defeat.

Yet daily served was he with care,
To soothe his wild, morose estate:
The garden’s crispest lettuce fair,
And golden oats upon his plate.

No ravenous hound pursued his heel,
No poacher snared him in the glade;
Yet Time’s relentless, quiet wheel
Has low his furry body laid.

Farewell, my grim, ungrateful friend!
Eight years of wrath have passed away;
I mourn thy strange, eccentric end,
And miss thy scowl at break of day.

### 1. "Epitaph on a Hare" by William Cowper (1784)

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue,
Nor shock of gunshot e’er annoy,
The happiest hare that ever fed
On leafy greens, a poet's joy.

Old Tiney, surliest of his kind,
Who, nursed with tender care,
Did oblige me, though he were inclined
To snap at his preserver’s hair.

Eight years I entertained him much,
At evening, when his sports began,
He’d leap and bound with nimble touch,
Beyond the wildest feats of man.

A Turkey carpet was his lawn,
Whereon he loved to bound and skip;
Their sugar-plums at early dawn
He took from many a friendly lip.

He died at last, old age his foe,
No lingering sickness laid him low;
Without a groan, without a sigh,
He laid him down and came to die.

Here lies old Tiney; gently tread,
Upon his bed of velvet moss;
A braver heart was never dead,
Nor left a kinder friend in loss.

---

### 2. A Short Modern Epitaph for a Hare

Beneath the clover, soft and deep,
The silent runner falls asleep.
No hound shall break his quiet rest,
No winter chill his grassy nest.

With velvet ears and watchful eyes,
Beneath the open meadow skies,
The swiftest heart upon the lea
Has found its peace beneath the tree.

Rest gently now, small timid friend,
Where green fields stretch without an end.

counterfactuals.prompt: What is a famous classic poem written about a pet hare? Can you paste the text?
counterfactuals.output:
The most famous classic poem about a pet hare is **"Epitaph on a Hare"** by the English poet **William Cowper** (1731–1800), written in 1783. 

Cowper famously kept three rescue hares named **Puss, Tiney, and Bess** to help him cope with severe bouts of depression. He built them housing, let them run around his carpeted parlor, and wrote extensively about them in his prose and poetry. "Epitaph on a Hare" was written upon the death of Tiney, who lived with Cowper for nearly nine years.

Here is the text of the poem:

***

### **Epitaph on a Hare**
*by William Cowper*

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue,
Nor swifter greyhound follow,
Nor sound of horn to cheer his crew,
Nor huntsman’s jovial hollo.

A turkey carpet was his lawn,
Whereon he loved to bound,
To skip and gambol like a fawn,
And play his frolic round.

His frisking was at evening hours,
For then he woke and stirred;
To feed on apples, twigs, and flowers,
Was what he much preferred.

For him the jasmine spread its flowers,
The lilac and the rose;
And when his juicy salads failed,
Sliced carrot pleased his nose.

His creeping vigour did not cease,
As years rolled swift away;
His coat was glossy to the last,
Forestalling decay.

Old Tiney, surliest of his kind,
Who parted with his spleen,
Was never reconciled to mind
Not even when he was green.

I kept him for his humour's sake,
For he would oft beguile
My heart of thoughts that made it ache,
And force me to a smile.

But now beneath this walnut shade
He finds his long repose,
The turf upon his ashes laid,
No adversary knows.

He died at last in order fit,
A natural death, of course;
He died of nothing but a fit
Of twitching, and remorse.

Eight years I kept him as my own,
And he would fain have stayed,
But, ah! his longevity was gone,
His debt of nature paid.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem mourning a tame jack-hare that was notoriously grumpy and loved to gambol on a Turkey carpet before rainstorms, ending with a reference to his burial beneath a walnut tree.
counterfactuals.output:
No gentle creature was this jack,
With frosted ears and coat of grey;
A sullen grump who turned his back
On all who sought to bid good day.
He’d thump his heel in cross disdain,
And nip the hand that proffered treats—
A hare of proud and moody strain,
Unhumbled by our indoor sheets.

Yet when the heavy air turned cold,
And thunder rumbled in the west,
A sudden magic would unfold
Within his sour, storm-struck chest.
Before the skies loosed down their rain,
He’d bound into the parlor room,
To shake away his old disdain
And dance against the gathering gloom.

Upon the Turkey carpet spread—
All woven rich in wool and red—
He’d leap and gambol, wild and free,
A burst of frantic ecstasy!
He’d twist his spine and kick his heels,
With flying paws and flashing eyes,
Releasing all the joy he feels
Before the dark rain split the skies.

Now clouds hang low and skies grow grey,
The rain taps softly on the glass,
Yet no mad hare leaps up today
To watch the storm-winds rise and pass.
The carpet lies so still and bare,
Unruffled by those thumping feet;
We miss the scowl he used to wear,
His surly grace, both wild and sweet.

We’ve wrapped him in a quiet sleep,
Far from the thunder's sudden call,
And dug a hollow, cool and deep,
Beside the old stone garden wall.
There let him rest, his gambols done,
From moody scowls and tempests free,
Laid softly, 'neath the fading sun,
To sleep beneath the walnut tree.
